title: The 9/11 attacks and the crisis of global liberalism
gist: Yglesias argues the Iraq and Afghanistan wars were an expression of liberal universalism rather than its opposite, which is why their failure is a major origin point of today's crisis of global liberalism — and why any liberal revival must be led by people too young to be complicit in it.

insights.claim: The failure of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars is, in an important way, one of the major origin points of the contemporary crisis of global liberalism.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Frames the retreat of the liberal international order as endogenous — caused by liberalism's own overreach rather than by external challengers.
insights.quote: The failure of those wars is, in an important way, one of the major origin points of the contemporary crisis of global liberalism.
insights.locator: The grandiose vision of democratizing the world at gunpoint

insights.claim: Bush's solidarity with American Muslims and his project of democratizing the world at gunpoint were two faces of the same coin — both expressions of liberal ideals about democracy, human rights, and universal values.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes the neocon era as a liberal project, which reorders how one reads today's realignment of foreign-policy factions.
insights.quote: The grandiose vision of democratizing the world at gunpoint, however deeply misguided, was in a very real sense an expression of liberal ideals about democracy and human rights and universal values.
insights.locator: An argument I make on the podcast

insights.claim: It is no coincidence that many leading neocon foreign-policy hawks of the 2000s later became prominent dissenters from the Republican Party's MAGA turn.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains the durable split inside the GOP foreign-policy establishment — useful for reading which factions will resist an isolationist policy turn.
insights.locator: just as it’s no coincidence that many of the leading “neocon”

insights.claim: A liberal revival will have to be led by people who were not adults in 2001 and can learn from the era's mistakes without being tainted by complicity in them.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Points to a generational handover as the precondition for any credible liberal internationalist comeback — a multi-cycle, not near-term, thesis.
insights.locator: It’s why I think a revival will ultimately have to be led

insights.claim: One prospective 9/11 hijacker was arrested before the attack, but the F.B.I. failed to crack the case partly because the legal standard at the time made it hard to get a warrant to search his laptop.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A single procedural constraint stood between the world's most consequential attack and its prevention — the canonical argument used to justify post-9/11 surveillance expansion.
insights.locator: The plot itself was by no means foreordained to succeed

insights.claim: Two hijackers had been positively identified as al-Qaeda associates by the C.I.A. and still entered the United States on lawful visas.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Interagency information failure, not absent intelligence, enabled the attack — the structural argument behind the entire homeland-security apparatus build-out.
insights.locator: Two hijackers had been positively identified

insights.claim: Had the plot been foiled, a response would still have been warranted but the emotional and political impact would have been dramatically reduced and the national-security response completely different.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The scale of the policy response tracked the emotional shock, not the underlying threat level — a general rule for forecasting post-crisis policy magnitude.
insights.locator: If the attack had been foiled

insights.claim: Had the attack occurred under an Al Gore administration, the immediate politics would likely have turned on the failure to prevent it rather than a hawkish politics of national unity.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Who holds the presidency when a shock lands determines whether it produces blame politics or rally-around-the-flag escalation.
insights.locator: It also seems likely that if the attack had occurred

insights.claim: Mass repeated exposure to atrocity footage drives ideological overshoot that later looks inexplicable — the same mechanism links 2001 war fever to 2020-vintage takes after the George Floyd video.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A reusable model for predicting policy overshoot after any nationally televised shock, and for anticipating the subsequent backlash phase.
insights.locator: But I do want to beg for the mercy of younger progressives

insights.claim: The contingencies behind almost any major historical event are shocking, per the co-host's observation on the episode — history is far less determined than retrospective accounts imply.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Argues against structural-determinist macro narratives; scenario weights should stay wide even for seemingly inevitable outcomes.
insights.quote: Every time you read about almost any major event in U.S. history or in world history or whatever, the contingencies are really shocking.

insights.claim: The counterargument acknowledged on the episode is that nothing about liberalism or cosmopolitan values suggests responding to a terrorist attack by attacking a country that had nothing to do with it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Marks the limit of the 'Iraq as liberal project' thesis — the good-faith framing of the war's architects remains contested.
insights.locator: Jerusalem pushes back on the effort to impute so much good faith

insights.claim: Bush used the agenda-setting power of the presidency to fuse a hawkish agenda with expressive maximalism about human equality and the universal appeal of liberal values, and both the world and the cause of liberalism are still paying the price.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Identifies presidential framing power as the transmission channel from a security shock to a decades-long ideological cost.
insights.locator: Bush used the considerable agenda-setting power
